'''Peter David Lax''' (1 May 1926 – 16 May 2025) was a Hungarian-born American mathematician and [[Abel Prize]] laureate working in the areas of [[Pure mathematics|pure]] and [[applied mathematics]].

Lax made important contributions to [[integrable system]]s, [[fluid dynamics]] and [[shock wave]]s, [[soliton]]ic physics, [[hyperbolic conservation laws]], and mathematical and [[scientific computing]], among other fields. In a 1958 paper Lax stated a [[conjecture]] about [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] representations for third-order hyperbolic polynomials which remained unproven for over four decades. Interest in the "Lax conjecture" grew as mathematicians working in several different areas recognized the importance of its implications in their field, until it was finally proven to be true in 2003.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lewis|first1=Adrian S.|last2=Parrilo|first2=Pablo A.|last3=Ramana|first3=Motakuri V.|year=2005|title=The Lax conjecture is true|journal=[[Proc. Amer. Math. Soc.]]|volume=133|issue=9|pages=2495–2499|arxiv=math/0304104|doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-05-07752-X|mr=2146191|s2cid=17436983}}</ref>

==Personal life and education==
Lax was born on 1 May 1926 in [[Budapest]], [[Kingdom of Hungary|Hungary]],<ref name=nytimesObit /> to a [[Jewish]] family.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Peter-Lax |title = Peter Lax &#124; Hungarian-American mathematician}}</ref> He began displaying an interest in mathematics at age twelve, and soon his parents hired [[Rózsa Péter]] as a tutor for him.<ref name="mmp" /> His parents Klara Kornfield and Henry Lax were both physicians and his uncle Albert Kornfeld (also known as Albert Korodi) was a mathematician, as well as a friend of [[Leó Szilárd]]. The family left Hungary on 15 November 1941 during [[World War II]], and traveled via [[Lisbon]] to the United States. 

As a student at [[Stuyvesant High School]], Lax took no math classes but did compete on the school math team. During this time, he met with [[John von Neumann]], [[Richard Courant]], and [[Paul Erdős]], who introduced him to [[Albert Einstein]]. As he was still 17 when he finished high school, he could avoid military service, and was able to study for three semesters at [[New York University]]. He attended a [[complex analysis]] class in the role of a student, but ended up taking over as instructor. He met his future wife, [[Anneli Cahn Lax|Anneli Cahn]] (married to her first husband at that time) in this class.<ref name="mmp" /><ref name="conv" />

Before being able to complete his studies, Lax was drafted into the U.S. Army. After basic training, the Army sent him to [[Texas A&M University]] for more studies. He was then sent to [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]], and soon afterwards to the [[Manhattan Project]] at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos]], [[New Mexico]]. At Los Alamos, he began working as a calculator operator, but eventually moved on to higher-level mathematics.<ref>{{cite book
 | last = Hersh | first = Reuben
 | doi = 10.1090/mbk/088
 | isbn = 978-1-4704-1708-6
 | location = Providence, Rhode Island
 | mr = 3243612
 | page = 24
 | publisher = American Mathematical Society
 | title = Peter Lax, mathematician
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=ammxBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA24
 | year = 2015}}</ref>

After the war ended, Lax remained with the Army at Los Alamos for another year, while taking courses at the [[University of New Mexico]], then studied at [[Stanford University]] for a semester with [[Gábor Szegő]] and [[George Pólya]].<ref name="mmp" /> Lax returned to NYU for the 1946–1947 academic year, and by pooling credits from the four universities at which he had studied, he graduated that year. He stayed at NYU for his graduate studies, marrying Anneli in 1948 and earning a PhD in 1949 under the supervision of [[Kurt O. Friedrichs]].<ref name="mmp">{{citation|contribution=Peter D. Lax|title=More Mathematical People|editor1-first=Donald J.|editor1-last=Albers|editor2-first=Gerald L.|editor2-last=Alexanderson|editor2-link=Gerald L. Alexanderson|editor3-first=Constance|editor3-last=Reid|editor3-link=Constance Reid|publisher=Harcourt Brace Jovanovich|year=1990|pages=138–159}}.</ref><ref name="conv">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/03/29/science/29conv.html |title=A Conversation with Peter Lax – From Budapest to Los Alamos, a Life in Mathematics |first=Claudia |last=Dreifus |author-link=Claudia Dreifus |date=29 March 2005 |work=The New York Times|access-date=31 October 2007}}</ref> After Anneli's death in 1999, Lax married Courant's daughter, Lori Berkowitz.<ref name=nytimesObit/>

==Career==
In 1954, the [[U.S. Atomic Energy Commission]] put Lax and several of his colleagues at NYU in charge of using an early [[supercomputer]] to calculate the risk of flooding for a major nuclear reactor if a nearby dam were sabotaged; they concluded that the reactor would be safe.<ref name=nytimesObit />

Lax made contributions to the theory of [[hyperbolic partial differential equation]]s. He made breakthroughs in understanding [[shock wave]]s from bombs, [[weather prediction]] and [[aerodynamic design]].<ref name=nytimesObit />

Concepts that bear Lax's name include the [[Lax equivalence theorem]], which explained when numerical computer approximations would be reliable, and [[Lax pair]]s, which are helpful in understanding the motion of [[soliton]]s. With [[Ralph Phillips (mathematician)|Ralph Phillips]], Lax developed the Lax-Phillips semigroup in [[scattering theory]], which explained how [[wave]]s move around obstacles and showed how to use the pattern of a wave's frequencies to understand its motion. That theory is helpful in [[Radar signal processing|processing radar signals]].<ref name=nytimesObit />

Lax held a faculty position in the Department of Mathematics, [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]], [[New York University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Peter D. Lax |url=https://math.nyu.edu/faculty/lax/ |access-date=2 March 2023 |website=math.nyu.edu}}</ref> Beginning in 1963, Dr. Lax directed the Courant Institute's computing facilities.<ref name=nytimesObit />

Lax died of [[cardiac amyloidosis]] at his Manhattan home, on 16 May 2025, at the age of 99.<ref name=nytimesObit>{{citation |last1=Barany|first1=Michael J.|last2=Shields|first2=Brit|title=Peter Lax, Pre-eminent Cold War Mathematician, Dies at 99 | newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=16 May 2025 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/16/science/peter-lax-dead.html | access-date=22 May 2025}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
He was a member of the [[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dnva.no/c26849/artikkel/vis.html?tid=40116|title=Gruppe 1: Matematiske fag|publisher=[[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]]|language=no|access-date=7 October 2010|archive-date=10 November 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131110152102/http://www.dnva.no/c26849/artikkel/vis.html?tid=40116|url-status=dead}}</ref> and the [[National Academy of Sciences, USA]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=Peter D. Lax|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/peter-d-lax-qx0cix/|access-date=29 June 2026|publisher=National Academy of Sciences}}</ref> the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=Peter David Lax|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/peter-david-lax|access-date=13 December 2021|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences}}</ref> and the [[American Philosophical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Peter+D.+Lax&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=13 December 2021|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> He won a [[Lester R. Ford Award]] in 1966<ref>{{cite journal|author=Lax, Peter D.|title=Numerical solutions of partial differential equations|journal=Amer. Math. Monthly|volume=72, Part II|issue=2|year=1965|pages=78–84|url=http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/writing-awards/numerical-solutions-of-partial-differential-equations|doi=10.2307/2313313 |jstor=2313313}}</ref> and again in 1973.<ref name="shockdecay">{{cite journal|author=Lax, Peter D.|title=The formation and decay of shock waves|journal=Amer. Math. Monthly|volume=79|issue=3|year=1972|pages=227–241|url=http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/writing-awards/the-formation-and-decay-of-shock-waves|doi=10.2307/2316618|jstor=2316618}}</ref> In 1974, his shock wave article<ref name="shockdecay"/> also won the [[Chauvenet Prize]]. He was awarded the [[National Medal of Science]] in 1986, the [[Wolf Prize]] in 1987, the [[Abel Prize]] in 2005 and the [[Lomonosov Gold Medal]] in 2013.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ras.ru/win/db/award_dsc.asp?P=id-1.ln-en|title=Большая золотая медаль РАН имени М.В. Ломоносова}}</ref> The [[American Mathematical Society]] selected him as its Gibbs Lecturer for 2007.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Lax, Peter D.|title=Mathematics and physics|journal=[[Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.]]|volume=45|issue=1|pages=135–152|mr=2358380|doi=10.1090/s0273-0979-07-01182-2|year=2008|doi-access=free}}</ref> In 2012, he became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 27 January 2013.</ref>

Lax is listed as an [[ISI highly cited researcher]].<ref>{{Cite web
  | last = Thomson ISI
  | title = Lax, Peter D., ISI Highly Cited Researchers
  | url= http://hcr3.isiknowledge.com/author.cgi?&link1=Browse&link2=Results&id=3419
  | access-date =20 June 2009}}
</ref> According to [[György Marx]], he was one of the Hungarian-American scientists known as [[The Martians (scientists)|The Martians]].<ref>[http://fizikaiszemle.hu/archivum/fsz9703/marsl.html A marslakók legendája -] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220409175959/http://fizikaiszemle.hu/archivum/fsz9703/marsl.html |date=9 April 2022 }} [[György Marx]]</ref>

Lax also received an Honorary Doctorate from [[Heriot-Watt University]] in 1990.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www1.hw.ac.uk/graduation/honorary-graduates.htm|title=Heriot-Watt University Edinburgh: Honorary Graduates|last=|website=www1.hw.ac.uk|access-date=4 April 2016|archive-date=18 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160418163907/http://www1.hw.ac.uk/graduation/honorary-graduates.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==The CDC 6600 incident==
In 1970, as part of an anti-war protest, the [[Transcendental Students]] took hostage a [[CDC 6600]] [[super computer]] at [[NYU]]'s [[Courant Institute]] which Lax had been instrumental in acquiring; the students demanded $100,000 in ransom ({{Inflation|US|100000|1970|fmt=eq|r=-4}}) to provide bail for a member of the [[Black Panthers]]. Some of the students present attempted to destroy the computer with incendiary devices, but Lax and colleagues managed to disable the devices and save the machine.<ref name=siam>{{cite web|title=Peter Lax|work=The History of Numerical Analysis and Scientific Computing |first=Philip |last=Colella |date=26 April 2004 |publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics |url=http://history.siam.org/oralhistories/lax.htm|author-link=Philip Colella }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | last=Barron | first=James | title=The Mathematicians Who Saved a Kidnapped N.Y.U. Computer | newspaper=The New York Times | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/12/07/nyregion/the-mathematicians-who-ended-the-kidnapping-of-an-nyu-computer.html | date=7 December 2015}}</ref>
